feedback.problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{10}($
{{field-1}} $)$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by  $I=\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that 

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-4x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{-4x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-4x})\,(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))-\int (-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))(-4{e}^{-4x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2J.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate

$$
J=\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To do this, let's suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}u={e}^{-4x}\, & ⇒\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{-4x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⇒\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}J & =\int {e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =({e}^{-4x})\,(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))-\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))(-4{e}^{-4x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2I.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2I) \\ I & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-4I \\ 5I & =-{e}^{-4x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)) \\ I & =-\frac{{e}^{-4x}}{10}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =(-\frac{{e}^{-4x}}{10}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(-\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{10}(0+1))-(-\frac{1}{10}(0+1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}-\frac{{e}^{-4\pi }}{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(1-{e}^{-4\pi }).\end{aligned}
$$
